constitutive_assumptions: Linear elastic behavior for the contacting bodies.
Elastic similarity between contacting bodies (Dundurs' parameter beta equals zero), decoupling normal pressure from shear traction distributions.
Poisson's ratio effects on transverse shear tractions are neglected, treating tangential energy release rate as pure mode II.
Initial contact gap is spherical/quadratic, consistent with Hertzian contact assumptions.
Coulomb friction law holds within the slip region with a constant sliding friction coefficient.
Slip initiation at the stick-slip boundary is governed by a Griffith energy release rate criterion / critical mode II stress intensity factor.
Direct normal adhesion is neglected, assuming classical normal adhesion is eliminated by surface roughness.
control_variables: Dimensionless toughness parameter / critical stick size ratio (c_c / a or c_c0 / a)
Contact pressure ratio relative to reference pressure (p_0 / p_0,nom) in the pressure-dependent model
dependent_variables: Stick zone radius (c) and stick-to-contact radius ratio (c / a)
Shear traction distribution q_x(r) across the interface
Critical stick zone radius c_c (and pressure-corrected critical radius c_c')
Threshold tangential load to initiate microslip (Q_min)
Peak tangential load prior to global sliding instability (Q_max) / apparent static friction coefficient
Mode II stress intensity factor (K_II) at the stick-slip boundary

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The transition from stick to slip in Hertzian contact can be modeled by superposing Hertzian contact pressure and a mode II singular adhesive solution analogous to JKR theory, where slip inception follows a Griffith fracture criterion while sliding follows Coulomb friction.

The Griffith friction model predicts that the stick zone remains larger than predicted by classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory and collapses abruptly into global sliding when reaching a critical stick zone size analogous to JKR pull-off.

The apparent static friction coefficient before sliding can significantly exceed the sliding friction coefficient, exhibiting size and normal load dependencies governed by the friction fracture energy.

Experimental measurements in PMMA interfaces show that local shear-to-normal stress ratios can reach values several times higher than the macroscopic static friction coefficient without precipitating slip, with strain fields consistent with shear crack fracture mechanics.
Incorporating a contact-pressure-dependent friction toughness accounts for variations in real contact area and alters the stick zone scaling across varying pressure regimes.

Historical experimental data for spherical contacts under oscillating tangential loads reveal stick zones 10-20% larger than classical Cattaneo-Mindlin predictions and non-cubic energy dissipation scaling, consistent with fracture mechanics-based stick-slip models.

future_work: Developing criteria to reliably select appropriate physical constants for cohesive/fracture models of friction from experimental data.
Extending the singular adhesive contact framework to more general non-axisymmetric contact geometries.
Further investigating whether interfacial roughness effects or fracture mechanics models better explain observed deviations in frictional energy dissipation under oscillating loads.
independent_variables: Mode II friction fracture energy (gamma) or nominal fracture energy (gamma_nom)
Radial position (r) within the contact area
limitations_inferred: The formulation is restricted to isotropic linear elastic materials and ideal spherical geometries, requiring modifications for compliant, viscoelastic, or highly deformable materials common in soft robotics.
The model assumes an idealized singular crack tip without an extended cohesive process zone, which may become inaccurate when stick zones approach asperity-scale dimensions.
Dynamic slip propagation velocity, interfacial wear, frictional heating, and slip-rate-dependent friction evolution are not modeled within this quasi-static framework.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model is quasi-static and does not account for viscoelastic and dynamic effects observed during interfacial slip propagation.
The spherical contact geometry analyzed differs significantly from the flat, sharp-edged geometries typically used in laboratory friction experiments.
Poisson's ratio effects are neglected by assuming shear stresses act purely parallel to the applied tangential load direction.
Exact analytical formulation is straightforward only for axisymmetric contacts; elliptical and more complex geometries require approximations.
The choice of reference nominal fracture energy at peak pressure is arbitrary.
Estimating physical constants for cohesive or fracture models remains uncertain due to large discrepancies in measured local shear-to-normal stress ratios.
main_results: Complete stick is maintained up to a non-zero threshold tangential load (Q_min), unlike classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory where microslip initiates immediately upon tangential loading.
Beyond the threshold load, the stick zone remains larger than the classical Cattaneo-Mindlin prediction for equivalent tangential loads.
When the stick region decreases to a critical size (c_c), force-controlled equilibrium becomes unstable, triggering a sudden transition to global sliding.

The peak tangential load prior to sliding can exceed the dynamic sliding limit (f * P) by up to a factor of 2 for partial-slip solutions, offering an explanation for the difference between static and dynamic friction coefficients.
Assuming constant friction fracture energy introduces contact size and normal load dependence into the apparent static friction coefficient.
Modifying the model with a pressure-dependent toughness retains the enlarged stick zone and critical drop to sliding, though the effect is attenuated at low pressures.
modeling_methods: Superposition method extending the Cattaneo-Mindlin tangential contact formulation.
Classical Hertzian contact pressure theory for spherical normal contact.
Mode II fracture mechanics formulation using the JKR adhesive contact solution for the corrective shear traction distribution in the stick zone.
Amontons-Coulomb friction law applied within the slip annulus.
Linearly pressure-dependent fracture toughness model accounting for real contact area variations.
Bounded asymptotic stress intensity factor analysis at the stick-slip boundary.
performance_metrics: Critical stick zone radius ratio (c_c / a and c_c' / a)
Tangential load enhancement factor before global sliding (Q_max / (f * P))
possible_gap_implications: Insights into the fracture-mechanics-governed transition from stick to slip and critical stick size instabilities could inform traction, grasping stability, and slip-onset models in compliant robotic grippers and contact interfaces, provided large deformations and viscoelasticity are incorporated.
Fracture mechanics descriptions of static friction enhancement and energy dissipation could improve contact compliance and fretting wear models in continuum joint mechanisms.
paper.research_objective: To formulate an analytical model for the Cattaneo-Mindlin problem of a Hertzian contact by introducing a Griffith fracture mechanics condition for the inception of slip in the stick region while preserving Coulomb friction in the slip region, investigating both constant and pressure-dependent friction fracture energy.
paper.research_problem: Classical Cattaneo-Mindlin theory based on Amontons-Coulomb friction predicts instantaneous microslip upon tangential loading and load-independent friction coefficients, which fails to capture fracture-mechanics-type singular shear stresses, elevated local friction ratios, stick-zone enlargement, and abrupt transitions from static to dynamic friction observed experimentally and in fault mechanics.
paper.title: Transition from stick to slip in Hertzian contact with “Griffith” friction: The Cattaneo–Mindlin problem revisited
